#10556. What we've been playing - "Shoving Moon Flesh into an alien grandma's mouth"

A few of the things that have us hooked this week.

Hello, it is me, your regular weekend host Mertie and I am here once again to guide you gently into Saturday with our usual feature What We've Been Playing, where we write a little about the games we've been, yes, playing. This week, Bertie - before fleeing for a well-deserved break and leaving me with the keys to the place - runs a one-on-one D&D game; Connor plays with his Moon Flesh in Warframe, and I've been serenely gallivanting over yonder hills.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

I'm a little busy outside of work at the moment with rehearsals for a play I'm in (The Importance of Being Ernest), but I did find time for another Dungeons & Dragons first: a one-on-one game. I've been wanting to do one of these for a while, and, as I discovered recently, one-on-one games are a whole thing. Duets, they're called, rather poetically. You need to modify campaigns a bit to be playable this way, because most are designed for groups of four or five people, and you probably need to give a player a companion character as backup. But otherwise, it's totally doable. Some people make adventures exclusively for one-on-one games.

I ran a mini-adventure called D8 Night, created by the now-closed dice shop Dakota Irish. It's a nice, warm two-hour-or-so affair, where the player is caught in a time-stilled village and tasked by some magical mischief maker to retrieve the components of a romantic meal before being allowed to leave. It's a simple enough set-up, and as with a lot of things D&D, the set-up doesn't really matter so much as the playing of it and the unexpected things that happen. And unexpected things did happen. I played with my partner so I know her likes pretty well, I like to think - that's the attraction of a one-on-one set-up like this - but I didn't expect her to connect so strongly with some of the incidental characters. This resulted in entire areas being imagined-to-life that weren't written on paper. The imagination never ceases to amaze me.

Anyway, I'm off to Comic Con this weekend to celebrate my birthday - it'll be my birthday when you're reading this. I'm off to geek-out about Critical Role and watch the new Laika animated film, and to stuff my face with food.

I had a lovely time playing developer Funselektor's Art of Rally follow-up Over the Hill last week, roaming its beautifully stylised wilderness expanses in my cheerful 4x4 so I could write some words about it all. But it clearly got its hooks into me, and I went on to spend pretty much my entire Saturday just pootling around the Canadian Valhallas, the Algerian desert, thoroughly transfixed by the tranquil rhythms of it all.

It really is a game for the curious - and the infinitely patient. As the old meme goes: See that mountain?, you can climb it. Just be prepared for a lot of slow-going, a lot of trial-and-error, and a lot of determination. But while it should be frustrating, the opposite somehow ends up being true, and it's easy to feel at peace in this striking wilderness, guitars strumming gentle encouragement as you become one with the world.

You haven't experienced FOMO until you've experienced MMO do-this-or-you'll-never-be-able-to-do-it-again FOMO: The once-in-a-lifetime grinds, the cosmetics that may be vaguely impressive to onlookers in a decade's time, and the first-thing-in-the-morning, last-thing-at-night routines of logging on and doing busywork.

For those unaware, Warframe is currently bracing for a journey into a whole new galaxy. The trip requires fuel, but given we're talking about the big-red-number-loving, fashion-forward, weirdly wonderful Warframe here, this fuel isn't diesel. No, Warframe players in their thousands are currently shoving Moon Flesh into an alien grandma's mouth.

We're taking parts of Eris - a grim petri dish home to countless infested ghouls - and, fouler still, the Mesa warframe. Like a ripe cheese, its stink is what meemaw craves, and providing it brings great rewards. These include weapons and dead-handy consumables like Legendary Cores and Archon Shards, but perhaps more delectable are the cosmetics. Some must be unlocked through a community-wide effort, while others are available to buy with Moon Flesh from the jump. And, of course, once the event ends, these will never return. Never ever.

I've been waking up at 6am everyday and doing missions for this Moon Flesh, and I've been doing it before bed as well. I, like many hopeless MMO/-live service players, am petrified that something in the game may never be mine to hoard. It has cut into my gym time, my morning coffee time, and indeed my sleep time. I owe my recent spree of unsubtle yawns in morning team meetings to Warframe. That's either a glowing endorsement, or a sign I need to ease up on this stuff. Who knows?

Am I allowed two entries? I'm not actually sure, but Bertie's not here to stop me so... ALSO, I have found myself consumed by Switch Sports Resort this week in a way I absolutely wasn't expecting to be when I fired it up for review. In my head, Nintendo's long-running series has always very much been a party game first, and an engaging solo endeavour a distant second.

But Switch Sports Resort is a bit of a treasure, and I've been having a great time with it on my own: taking it online for a bit of ranked or casual play, working through some achievements, or just firing up one of its fantastic open-world sightseeing modes for a leisurely explore. I hope Nintendo's got some post-launch plans in the works, because I'd love for it to go a little bit harder with the open-world stuff, particularly where flying is concerned. But until then there's skateboarding, which is bloody brilliant, and I'm already craving more.

#10555. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected

A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially important because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

The researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

By contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#10553. Influencer who flaunted private jets indicted over alleged $4 million food stamp fraud scheme

A social media influencer has been arrested after allegedly stealing millions of dollars from a government food assistance programme.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) provides financial support to those with low income, allowing eligible households to purchase groceries using electronic benefit transfer (EBT) cards.

Atlanta-based influencer Mercedes Reshard New, also known as Shawty Dred, has been accused of exploiting the scheme to obtain more than $4 million in benefits between January 2020 and July 2026.

According to the US Department of Justice, the 39-year-old allegedly created more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts using stolen identities, before arranging for EBT cards to be delivered to addresses across Atlanta.

Prosecutors also claim that New registered his business, Shawty Dred LLC, as an authorized SNAP retailer, allowing him to withdraw more than $660,000 through transactions involving the fraudulent cards.

After his retailer authorization was revoked in November 2025, New allegedly approached Walmart shoppers and offered to pay for their groceries using EBT cards in exchange for cash.

New was indicted on 63 federal charges, including mail fraud, aggravated identity theft and SNAP fraud, before being arrested on October 13.

During a court appearance on October 22, New pleaded not guilty and was denied bond, with prosecutors arguing that he posed a flight risk. He remains in custody awaiting further proceedings.

#10551. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 is more than a retread of Netflix's beloved first season - it's a story that truly understands what it means to exist in Night City

Last night, I sat down with a greasy pizza and a few bottles of beer and braced myself for 10 episodes of heartbreak. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' second season is out, and it follows in the footsteps of Studio Trigger's beloved, and tragic, debut. My expectations were way off.

Not because it wasn't good: Edgerunners Season 2 is fantastic. Packed with a wonderful cast of troubled characters, their story brought to life with gorgeous and often unorthodox animation. The soundtrack, the voice acting... Quality-wise the bar is as high as the first season. What surprised me was the decision to bring something many may find peculiar given Cyberpunk's dire setting and desperate energy. The show is hopeful. Defiant, even.

In the show's opening episode, we are introduced to characters at rock bottom. King, having suffered from cyberpsychosis, has had his augmentations stripped out of his body, and lost his home. D's in the midst of a lonely journey of revenge, while Talia is rubbing elbows with the Maelstrom gang. Roman, a 12-year-old, is broke and struggling to pursue filmmaking in a world that's left the medium behind. In the pursuit of money, he is nearly diced up.

These characters have all the reason in the world to lose themselves to despair, to burn out. Some almost do. However, as the season progresses, they each find a reason to push on, to live in spite of the odds. By the end of the season, while their problems may not have vanished, those who can choose to push on regardless of what life may throw at them. There are more smiles and laughs in the final episode than there are in the first. In the world of Cyberpunk, that's surprising. Defiant.

Violence in Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 is not treated as some awesome, cathartic spectacle. Through the literal lens of Roman, it's seen as the monstrous act it is. Characters are urged to not go out and kill people - even those who arguably deserve it - consistently throughout the show. In the first season, we saw the brutal reality of killing in David's descent into cyberpsychosis. In this season, characters without that particular affliction are confronted with the futility of the act.

Around halfway through the season, a cowering lady is half-heartedly executed by a side character, and the show lingers on the scene as her head slumps down onto the ground. It's a grisly moment, a siren blaring starkly, broadcasting a very simple message: violence is not the answer.

There is a sentiment that there are no good endings in Night City, and it's a fair belief to have. Magda Zych, senior writer at CD Projekt Red, described the game's story as a 'noir tragedy', and the dystopian world of the tabletop RPG presents a similarly sad motif. Crime is rampant, people are victimised for no reason, people are chewed up and spat out. This was true in Mike Pondsmith's original vision for Night City, it was true in Cyberpunk 2077, and it's true in Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2.

So there's courage in living as best you can in spite of the injustice of the world. If the first season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners could be aligned, roughly, to 2077's 'The Sun' ending (where V charges into Arasaka in a blaze of glory), Season 2 can be seen as a parallel to 'The Star' ending, where V takes what time they have left and spends it with their friends and loved ones, divorced from the grinding reality of Night City's grinding concrete. Some NPCs react to this decision during the credits with scorn; it is the antithesis of the 'burn bright, die young' Edgerunner philosophy.

I imagine this season may not have met the expectations of many viewers, who are left cold by how different it is from the first season. And yeah, it would have been entirely acceptable to rehash the same sort of story we saw in 2022 again here, and many people - including myself - would have loved it. But to choose not to do that, to steer the narrative into a totally different direction, is smart. You might even say... defiant.

#10550. Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a new way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

For the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an important part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

The new control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," says Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices."

The robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible."

The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

Choosing the best 3D animation software depends on your experience, budget, and creative goals. Some tools offer complete 3D modeling and animation workflows, while others specialize in professional character animation, visual effects, or AI-powered video creation. This guide compares five options and notes how each fits into web and game projects, so designers and developers can see which one suits their pipeline.

Blender is one of the strongest free options for anyone looking for comprehensive 3D animation software. This open-source application combines modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, rendering, simulation, and compositing in one package.

Blender provides a broad production workflow without requiring users to pay for a standard commercial license. Its active community, learning resources, and add-on ecosystem make it accessible to independent creators. It is suitable for everything from simple animated scenes to complex short films and game assets.

For web and game developers: Blender ships with a glTF 2.0 importer and exporter, and glTF is the format libraries such as three.js load for 3D on the web. See the Blender manual’s glTF page for export options.

Its extensive interface and feature set can feel overwhelming to new users. Learning advanced rigging, lighting, materials, and rendering takes time, and some established studios may have specialized pipelines built around other applications.

Beginners, freelancers, indie game developers, students, and professionals who need a powerful 3D animation tool without a software subscription.

Autodesk Maya is a professional 3D application widely associated with character animation, rigging, film production, and game development. It offers detailed control over character movement and complex animation workflows, making it a strong choice for artists working in established production environments.

Maya provides sophisticated tools for animating characters and managing complex scenes. Its established role in many professional workflows makes it a valuable skill for artists pursuing careers in film, television, and game development. It also offers detailed control over animation timing, character motion, and rig behavior.

Maya generally requires a paid subscription, which can be expensive for hobbyists and independent creators. Its advanced interface also takes time to learn, particularly for users who have never worked with professional 3D software.

Professional animators, film and television artists, game studios, and users who need advanced character animation and rigging capabilities.

Cinema 4D is a 3D modeling, animation, and rendering application known for its motion graphics workflow. It is widely used for commercial visuals, broadcast graphics, product animations, and creative work that combines 3D elements with graphic design.

Cinema 4D is a strong option for designers who want to create polished motion graphics and branded animation. Its MoGraph workflow can make repetitive or complex movements easier to manage, and its integration with common design workflows is helpful for agencies and creative teams.

For web and product designers: Cinema 4D includes a glTF exporter, which helps when a designer needs to hand a 3D model to a developer for the web. Maxon documents the options on its glTF export settings page.

Cinema 4D is a commercial product, so ongoing licensing costs may be a concern. Although it can handle a wide range of 3D work, users focused on highly specialized character animation or procedural visual effects may prefer tools designed around those workflows.

Motion designers, advertising agencies, broadcast artists, product visualization specialists, and creators who regularly produce animated graphics.

Houdini, developed by SideFX, is a 3D software package known for procedural workflows and advanced visual effects. Rather than relying entirely on manually created steps, artists can build systems that generate and modify complex scenes, simulations, and effects.

Houdini offers exceptional flexibility for technical artists and visual-effects specialists. Procedural workflows make it possible to create reusable systems and adjust complex effects efficiently. Its capabilities are particularly valuable when a project needs detailed simulations or large numbers of interconnected elements.

For game developers: SideFX offers Houdini Engine plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine, which let procedural Houdini assets be used inside those engines. SideFX explains the plugins in its Houdini Engine FAQ.

Houdini has a steep learning curve, especially for beginners who are unfamiliar with node-based workflows. Building effective procedural systems requires patience and technical understanding. While free learning options are available, some commercial uses and advanced workflows require an appropriate paid license.

Visual-effects artists, technical directors, simulation specialists, and experienced 3D creators working on demanding film, television, or game projects.

MagicLight.AI is different from the four tools above. It is an AI-powered video creation platform rather than a traditional 3D application, so it produces finished animated videos, not editable 3D scenes, rigs, or game assets. It is included here for readers who want animated storytelling without building a 3D pipeline. It supports AI-generated characters, scene creation, storyboarding, and voice features.

MagicLight.AI can reduce the time and technical effort needed to create animated videos. It is particularly useful for content creators, educators, marketers, and storytellers who want to focus on the script and final message rather than mastering a complex 3D production pipeline.

MagicLight.AI is not a replacement for dedicated 3D software when you need precise control over mesh topology, character rigs, keyframes, physics, or custom 3D scenes. Creators who need editable 3D assets for games or studio production will need a conventional 3D application such as the ones above.

Content creators, educators, and marketers who want to produce animated videos efficiently without learning a traditional 3D animation workflow.

The right software is the one that supports your actual production needs. Before choosing a tool, consider the following factors.

If you want to model objects, build character rigs, and control animation precisely, start with a dedicated 3D application such as Blender or Maya. If your goal is to create animated storytelling videos from scripts or ideas with less manual production work, an AI video tool such as MagicLight.AI may be a more convenient option.

Blender is an excellent starting point if you need a complete 3D toolset without a standard license fee. Houdini also has a free Apprentice edition with restrictions. Maya and Cinema 4D are commercial applications, so compare their current plans against your expected usage before committing.

Different applications suit different workflows. Blender is versatile, Maya excels at character animation, Cinema 4D is well suited to motion graphics, and Houdini is especially powerful for procedural effects. MagicLight.AI is better suited to AI-assisted video production than to detailed, manually controlled 3D scene creation.

Beginners may find Blender’s extensive learning resources helpful, although its broad feature set takes time to master. Maya and Houdini demand more specialized skills for advanced work, while Cinema 4D is often considered by motion designers seeking a more direct design-oriented workflow. AI video tools can reduce the amount of technical setup required, but still require creative direction and review.

Think about where the finished animation will be used. A web project may need a lightweight glTF model. A game project may require exportable 3D assets, rig compatibility, and a game-engine workflow. A commercial motion graphic may depend on rendering and compositing integration. A social video or animated explainer may prioritize turnaround time, narration, subtitles, and scene continuity.

The best 3D animation software in 2026 depends on your budget, experience, and intended output. Blender is the strongest starting point for many users who want a comprehensive free 3D workflow. Autodesk Maya is a compelling option for professional character animation, Cinema 4D suits motion graphics and commercial visuals, and Houdini stands out for procedural effects and complex simulations. MagicLight.AI offers a different approach: it helps creators generate animated videos with AI rather than manually building a traditional 3D production pipeline.

Blender is one of the best free options because it includes modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and other production tools in a single open-source application. It is suitable for beginners as well as experienced artists.

Yes. Free software can support professional-quality work when used effectively. Blender, for example, provides a comprehensive toolset for animation and rendering. The final result depends on the artist’s skills, project requirements, hardware, and production workflow.

Blender is a strong choice for beginners who want to learn traditional 3D modeling and animation without paying for a standard software license. Those who mainly want to create animated videos from stories or scripts may prefer exploring an AI video creation platform such as MagicLight.AI.

Blender and Cinema 4D can both export glTF, a format widely used for 3D on the web. Blender is free, so it is the easiest place to start.

#10547. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," said Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely new materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed."

Using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

That ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," said Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

"Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives."

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

This technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

"We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform."

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

The researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

The carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

The researchers also reported that the new system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

"Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power."

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics

The team now plans to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

"Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible."

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

#10546. Phantom Blade Zero review

I wasn't around to witness the golden age of Martial Arts cinema, but there are moments in Phantom Blade Zero that make me feel as though I've tumbled through a crack in time onto the set of a kung fu film. There's one particular encounter that sticks in my mind. Approaching a group of enemies in a shaded valley, I slowly raise my sword, and the first enemy rushes at me. Fool. I perfectly parry the blow, performing a slow-motion somersault to land behind him and plant my sword firmly in his back. The next guy comes running in, and I kick him in the face while simultaneously stabbing the previous enemy in the throat. A third joins the fray - this one on horseback - so I boot him off his horse, and use his steed to trample his helpless friend into the dust. Then, at last, there is silence.

This is Phantom Blade Zero at its absolute peak: cinematic, free-flowing, and full of surprises. Its combat channels the seamless motion and creative choreography of the very best kung fu films, with some frankly astonishing combat animations that seem almost limitless in their ingenuity and variety. It's a game of extraordinary beauty, with jaw-dropping landscapes and hugely ambitious combat encounters. If only - if only! - it could maintain this incredible level of fluidity in all areas of its epic tale.

Our adventure takes place in a fantastical, wuxia-flavoured world called the Wulin: a martial underworld where vicious ne'er-do-wells seem to be running riot, and generally making life miserable for regular people who are just trying to live their lives. Truly, a world miles apart from our own. You play as Soul, a warrior and outcast member of an organisation called The Order. Having played through the entirety of the game, I'm still not entirely sure what The Order stands for in terms of values, but I'm sure they originally meant well. I'm also not really sure what I can tell you about the story - we've been asked not to discuss anything that happens in the prologue - so you're all going to have to use your imaginations here. I can tell you it involves betrayal, a protagonist with limited days to live, a revenge mission, and various malevolent entities from another world. All the standard ingredients you need for a fantasy epic, really.

To warn you in advance, it doesn't take long for Phantom Blade Zero to start dumping an absolutely dizzying number of character names, bloodlines, cults and various feuding sects on you. The way the world lore is delivered - often through reams of text in collectible scrolls dotted around the Wulin - is definitely not one of Phantom Blade Zero's strengths. Most of the game's characters have much to say about nothing, offering various platitudes, truisms and declarations of values that are hard to connect with the underlying story. My advice is to just let everything wash over you, and you'll eventually pick up on the main plot points. While the narrative content leaves much to be desired, the storytelling does include some absolute visual treats - even utilising a traditional Chinese art form to do so. Unfortunately I can't actually praise this in full, because we were also asked not to discuss these elements in our reviews.

Anyway, I think we all know why we're here, and that's because the main draw of Phantom Blade Zero is its combat. The FromSoftware influence is evident in so many aspects of this game, from the series of 'bell' checkpoints scattered throughout the world, to the multi-stage bosses that, yes, can deliver one-shot attacks. Regardless of your weapon loadout, the most important thing you can do in a boss battle is correctly dodge red attacks, and parry blue ones. It's the single most effective way of breaking a boss's guard so that you can enter a punishment phase, and finally get your heavy-hitting moves in. It's kinda like high-octane Sekiro. So if you're not a fan of this dodge/parry combat style, this might not be the game for you.

Perhaps Soulslite would be the better term for Phantom Blade Zero, as there are a lot of clever adjustments here that allow for much speedier combat than other Soulslikes would permit. There isn't a traditional stamina bar, but instead a resource called 'sha-chi', which depletes when you block or parry enemy attacks and when you use heavy attacks. It's a nifty way to allow players to use quick attacks, sprints and dodges without costing stamina. Tied to this is Phantom Blade Zero's two-weapon system, which promotes regular switching between main weapons. If you're running low on sha-chi using one weapon, simply swap to the other and - ta dah! - you have a fresh sha-chi bar to work with (although there is a slight cooldown to prevent total abuse of this mechanic).

This is particularly useful when you want to get some heavy hits in, or if you need to prevent your guard from being broken, which happens when your sha-chi runs low. Another welcome adjustment is that the parry and dodge windows feel really quite generous, which is essential when enemies attacks are coming at you with such speed. If you need to do a last-minute parry, you can cancel nearly any of your moves to do so, which prevents that infuriating problem where you end up locked into an attack juuust as the boss raises their big meat cleaver right above your noggin. The greatest mercy of all is that if you're killed during the second phase of a boss fight, you can just re-enter the boss fight at the start of that second phase. It makes your failures slightly less heartbreaking, and gives you a chance to hop right back into the action with a full set of resources to play with.

Then there are the weapons themselves, which are incredibly flashy and give you access to some genuinely exciting abilities. One sword requires you to tank up on booze, then allows you to send the weapon flying around through the air to attack enemies at range - an enjoyably silly moveset which may not be the most effective build, but which is still fun to play nonetheless. Later you get pole-like swords that can charge through enemies, twin swords that rotate in orbit around you, and a weapon that can summon flowers out of the ground to drain an opponent's sha-chi. There's definitely a process of mastering these weapons and understanding how best to use their abilities in combat - particularly because each has its own unique combinations that are gradually unlocked as you find upgrade materials around the world. Eventually, you find quest items which allow you to 'soul temper' weapons to unlock their most powerful latent abilities, which can suddenly transform an underpowered weapon into something really quite viable (hello again, drunken sword). There's also a class of secondary weapons, known as phantom edges, which are intended for use as additional tools you can draw on in battle to solve problems like high boss guards or unblockable attacks. I constantly experimented with weapons to get a feel for them, and was able to fine-tune my build so that I had a loadout for dealing with large numbers of enemies, and another loadout for breaking boss guards. I got into a real rhythm with the combat, and knew exactly which order in which to pull my moves to maximise my damage.

Against regular enemies found around the Wulin, these weapons feel extraordinary. The combat achieves that perfect kung-fu flow state, and you can bounce around between enemies parrying their blows, lowering their guards, and opening them up for executions. I adore how generous Phantom Blade Zero is with these executions - hit a QTE at the right time, and you can take out two enemies at once. There also seems to be a never-ending supply of these animations: Soul will often use the enemy's own weapons against them, meaning you'll still be finding brand new execution moves 30 hours into the game. It makes the combat constantly surprising, giving variety to the encounters and encouraging you to be aggressive to unlock these deadly finishers. On the regular pathfinder difficulty, the normal enemies feel really well-balanced - you get that sense of flow, but it's absolutely still possible to mess things up if you go charging in without the right loadout, or without priorisiting ranged enemies first.

Against boss enemies, however, these once-powerful weapons are suddenly defanged. During my playthrough, a very high proportion of the bosses felt spongy - especially on pathfinder mode, but even if you lowered the difficulty to wayfarer, which is supposed to be the fun 'rampage through the game' difficulty setting. The weapons which felt so effective against other enemies suddenly became toothpicks against these bosses, even during their punishment phases. Successfully parrying or dodging was rewarded with a very minor dink to a boss's sha-chi, instantly giving you that sinking feeling that you're in for a very long, repetitive fight.

In a Soulslike game, low damage is normally a hint to start experimenting with your build or to try different weapons to see if you can find the 'key' to a boss fight, but Phantom Blade Zero is not very good at communicating exactly what these might be. As an example, one early obligatory boss fight sees you fight an enemy with a spiked shield, and attacking said enemy causes you to start bleeding. It's obvious that you need to break the shield, and that you need to use one of the game's secondary weapons to do so - but when you use the axe phantom edge, very little happens, and that lack of reactivity caused me to go back walking through the world thinking I'd missed something. Turns out I was on the right track, and just needed to keep spamming the move or do a 'charged' version of it (which the game doesn't exactly encourage, as the wind-ups for these charged phantom edge moves are so long that they're normally not viable in the middle of a fast-paced battle). In another case, a phantom edge which shoots water - and is specifically described as being effective against fire types - did absolutely nothing against a fire type enemy. I often didn't feel rewarded for testing these different phantom edges, and the sponginess of the bosses, particularly in the early to mid game when your build options are limited, made a lot of these battles feel artificially lengthy.

This is one of my main gripes with the game, but this is also where things get… interesting. Two days before the review embargo was due to lift, developer S-Game released a 67GB update targeting performance and bugs, along with boss, enemy, ability and weapon stats. "These changes aim to make the difficulty curve feel smoother, both in boss fights and as you progress through each area," we were told. Obviously, this did not give me time to replay the entire game to see if the changes made a difference to the overall experience. I did return to some old save files and found that the sponginess remained present in several boss fights - especially those early obligatory ones - so it appears to still be an issue. It's possible that the launch build will allow player parries, dodges and weapons to feel a little more effective against bosses - but alas, I can only write about the version of the game I've played.

Despite the variety of animations and move sets used by the bosses, a lot of these battles also seem to fall into a fairly strict defend/attack pattern where you don't have much opportunity to disrupt enemy movesets. But that's not to say all boss battles feel exactly the same. Those with multiple smaller enemies allow you to feel like you're doing more damage, while some of the most memorable battles break out of the standard pattern to bring in something totally different. One boss fires missiles horizontally like a bullet hell, while another sees you dance on top of poles while exchanging cannon fire with your enemy. The latter was absolutely fantastic: visually stunning, unexpected, and a moment of pure unadulterated fun.

Of course, an essential part of any Soulslike/lite is noodling around the world to find upgrades and blow off steam between boss fights, and praise should go to the exploration aspect of Phantom Blade Zero. The world map is formed of traditional hand-painted ink wash paintings, with mists that part to reveal new areas with each bell you discover. These beautiful maps only hint at what you'll encounter in each area: you have to find your way through by observing the landscape and spotting hidden pathways on foot. There are plenty of 'aha' moments where you finally find the way up to a distant chest on a cliff that you'd spotted a while back. The Metroidvania elements of the game similarly build anticipation for being able to return to an area, with the phantom edge weapons you unlock through the main story later giving you access to previously-locked areas. S-Game does occasionally overcook this by placing too many closed doors next to each other: on entering the game's main city, I encountered a cluster of seven locked areas within the first few streets, which was a bit dispiriting. No room at the inn for poor old Soul, it seems. My advice is to really take your time in your initial exploration of an area, and not rush to the next region until you're fairly certain you've explored as much as you can at that stage. It's hard to see from the world map what you might have missed - and because enemies don't respawn, retraversing through these levels later on can feel weirdly empty.

Phantom Blade Zero has some extraordinary highs, but a gradual build-up of niggles eventually starts to weigh on you during a playthrough. It's a death by a thousand cuts, of things that really should have been caught during play testing. There's an essential key that's easy to miss because it glows orange and is placed next to a fire of the same colour. It's easy to get caught on geometry, and you end up doing much of your fighting against walls when you push your enemies there with long-combination attack patterns. On several occasions bosses hopped outside their arenas to attack me from behind invisible walls - a sort of reverse cheese that I really didn't appreciate. Certain sidequest missions misdirected me on the map, leaving me going around in circles when it turns out an entirely unrelated quest needed to be completed first. I experienced some severe frame rate dips in certain areas of the game, too - not ideal for a fast-paced action game. These nuisances do stack up, and although S-Game said it has addressed the escaping bosses, performance issues and the quest guidance fails in its latest patch, it's hard to say conclusively whether all of these issues have been fully resolved. The frame rates do seem to be better since the update, but that annoying side quest loop is still in place.

On/off setting for motion blur and camera shake. Adjustable brightness options, two font size options. Independent sliders for music, effects and dialogue. Four difficulty settings. Control scheme screen easily available, full key and button remapping. Can invert Y/X axis. Adjustable controller vibration and sensitivity settings.

All of which leaves us with quite a tricky picture. This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Street fights with multiple opponents feel so cinematic and so satisfying, allowing you to be truly creative and expressive with your fighting style. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword. This slows the pace of the early to mid game in particular, and I wish S-Game had been prepared to speed us through to the real meat of its gameplay a little faster. Combined with the other smaller issues and niggles - plus the pretty unremarkable narrative and lore dumps - it just takes the shine off what is otherwise a very impressive action title. Who knows, maybe another patch or two will even things out. Because there are some incredibly fun weapons to play with here… if only they had been sharpened.

A copy of Phantom Blade Zero was provided for this review by S-Game.

#10545. Dead by Daylight team respond following backlash to TheBurntPeanut receiving free DLC

Dead by Daylight developer Behavior Interactive has responded to community backlash after gifting a popular Twitch streamer free DLC during a recent livestream.

TheBurntPeanut is an American gaming streamer who has become one of the biggest personalities on Twitch, known for his energetic commentary and distinctive animated peanut avatar.

The streamer was playing the multiplayer survival horror video game Dead by Daylight on stream when he was gifted free access to all of the game’s DLC characters and perks, prompting backlash from the community.

TheBurntPeanut joked that he was on the receiving end of “streamer privileges” after realizing he had been granted access. The game’s official Twitch account then responded by commenting, “WE CAN TAKE THE HEAT! THEY ARE YOURS TO KEEP,” as revealed in screenshots shared to Reddit.

This weekend, a Dead by Daylight team member awarded in-game content and currency to a creator streaming our game. Although it is not unusual to unlock content to give creators discovering DbD a chance to have a sneak peek at available content, this decision was made without…

Some fans of the game responded negatively to the incident, prompting a response from DbD Pulse, the game’s community page, on X. The post revealed that the decision to give TheBurntPeanut access was made without appropriate approvals.

“When concerns about this decision became apparent during the stream, we should have responded by looking into these concerns, not dismissing them,” the post reads. “Unfortunately, we’ve now seen the fallout of this decision unfolding in many conversations across the DbD community.”

The post claimed that the Dead by Daylight team were upset at the “inflammatory language” being used towards members of the community, and branded the threats being made toward employees as “unacceptable”.

“We apologize to our community for letting you down. We have already begun reviewing our internal processes to prevent an incident like this from happening again,” they concluded.

#10543. The 13 scariest, spookiest video games you should play this Halloween

The nights are drawing in, which can only mean one thing: more bed. But also the impending frights and sights of All Hallow's Eve. Yes, the season of good fear is upon us again, summoning visions of cardboard box robot costumes and other, more devilish things.

And in the spirit of it all, we've crowded around the ouija board to spirit up a list of our horror game favourites - playable on PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 & 2, and VR - that might just sate your macabre appetites this Halloween. Some are scary, some are grim, others offer milder - but no less spooky - chills. We'll be doing a smattering of other spooky stuff as the week goes on, but if you're looking for more recommendations, we did a different horror list last year. And if you've your own favourites, please do share them below!

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

Where better to start then with Resident Evil, one of the granddaddies of survival horror gaming? And Resident Evil Requiem is, as much as anything, a celebration of the series as it turns 30. If Resident Evil is a series of two halves - one part campy action, one part genuine scares - Requiem is the perfect tribute, and when it leans heavily into horror in its sublime opening hours, it's genuinely terrifying. New protagonist Grace Ashcroft is the perfect accompaniment as she leads these first-person segments, roaming a wonderfully atmospheric Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Centre and dealing with some very human zombies who, disturbingly, don't yet seem to realise they're dead. Then comes series stalwart Leon S. Kennedy, roundhouse kicking and quipping to ease the tension in intermittent third-person interludes before it's back into the scares. Eventually, the horror gives way to heavier action, but then go on the party hats for a final stretch of glorious fan-service that feels entirely deserved. It's not only a great Resi game, it's one of the best games this year.

Silent Hill, another grandaddy of the survival horror genre, has always been the moodier of the two big series, trading Resident Evil's B-movie thrills for quieter, more ambient psychological scares. And it's the same story with this year's Silent Hill Townfall, which - continuing the trend established by last year's marvellous Japan-set Silent Hill F - shifts the fog-shrouded action again, this time to a small Scottish island blighted by tragedy. Developer Screen Burn, known for the acclaimed likes of Stories Untold and Observation, takes some big swings here, trading the series' classic third-person perspective for a more intimate first-person one, and shifting the focus from erratic gunplay to stealth. It also tells an unexpectedly gritty and very British tale as it jumps between multiple protagonists. The result is an effective, affecting, and relentlessly suffocating piece of horror. It's not perfect, proving perhaps a bit too relentless, but few series remain this exciting, and so willing to reinvent themselves, after nearly three decades.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

What Little Nightmares originator Tarsier Studios did next. Having stepped away from the horror series that made its name a few years back, Tarsier returned earlier this year with a fresh macabre offering that, on paper at least, doesn't sound like much of a departure at all. Much like Little Nightmares, Reanimal follows the adventure of two lovable, spindly-limbed moppets - here, Boy and Girl - lost in a hellish, hostile world players traverse by scrambling over platforms, solving light puzzles, and fleeing horrifying entities during the big crescendo moments. What sets it apart, however, is the sumptuous cinematic flair of presentation and a much darker mood: in Reanimal, Little Nightmares' Burton-esque whimsy gives way to a bleaker, more vicious - and undoubtedly more violent - vision that's often genuinely disturbing. That darkness is somewhat alleviated by the comfort of two-player co-op, but however you choose to play, Tarsier's latest is a treat. A game of phenomenal mood and artistry, as striking as it is enigmatic, and a wonderfully grim accompaniment for Halloween.

If the name sounds familiar but the game does not, that might be because developer David Szymanski's Iron Lung was turned into a movie earlier this year by none other than YouTuber Markiplier. And even if you've seen the film adaptation, the original game is worth checking out; it's a masterclass in lo-fi horror that's quite unlike anything else. Early on, Iron Lung seals you into a squalid submersible and plunges you into a blood ocean on a distant alien world. Your goal is to chart its labyrinthine depths - an unknowable expanse of suffocating darkness and silence - searching for several points of interest. The problem? No windows. Instead, you're forced to rely on the tiny, murky image of the world outside beamed onto the submersible's TV screen; the darkness so overbearing, all you can see are the glimpses of strangeness caught in your floodlights. As such, movement becomes a game of blind micro-bursts and cautious rotations, as you sporadically consult your map. That's stressful enough, but Iron Lung plays some clever tricks; its stellar sound design increasingly suggesting something terrible lurks in the darkness. Slowly, the tension reaches suffocating, unbearable heights, and you'll frankly be glad it only takes 45-minutes or so to complete.

Ghost Town's biggest roadblock is the fact it's a VR-exclusive game. But if you've got the means to check it out, it's a gem. Ghost Town is the work of Fireproof Games, and it shares some similarities with the studio's earlier, acclaimed The Room series - particularly in its love of tactile puzzle boxes and contraptions. But Ghost Town is far more ambitious, building a propulsive urban fantasy adventure around its core puzzling, and plunging players into a brilliantly evocative recreation of 1983 London as protagonist and ghost hunter Edith Penrose hunts for her missing brother. As the grimy streets of the capital make way for the craggy seclusion of the North Sea, and, eventually, strange realms beyond, it's wonderfully spooky stuff - full of great writing, captivating world-building, endearing characters, fantastic puzzles, and some magnificently imaginative set-pieces - there's a bit with a lighthouse trapped in time thanks to a troubled spirit that's a real highlight. This one's for you if you've ever suspected dark arts were occurring on the London Underground.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

It's 1879 and you, private investigator Declan Ward, have been summoned to a remote, rain-lashed corner of western Ireland in search of a young woman named Evelyn Deane. It's a journey that brings you to the titular Blake Manor, now a grand hotel, where the turnips - historically accurate jack-o'-lanterns, if you were wondering - are out in force. We are, you see, three days from All Hallow's Eve, and the hotel is bustling with guests: spiritualists, mentalists, naysayers, and more; here to witness the Grand Séance and a never-before-seen attempt to commune with the dead. All, perhaps, also know something about Evelyn Dean's whereabouts. Soon enough, the detective work begins, and you 'll start sniffing around empty rooms and tantalising corners, searching for discarded notes, newspaper clippings, and other useful clues. You'll also want to interrogate the guests as they move around the house according to their hourly schedule. But every action nudges the clock on further, meaning you'll need to spend your time wisely as awful calamity approaches. Soon new secrets, new mysteries, begin to emerge, and as the clockwork rhythms of day make way for the nightmarish hallucinations of night, is anyone safe?

A tribute to a Doom modder's childhood friend, replicating the family home they used to play together in. As Myhouse.wad creator Veddge explained when he first shared the acclaimed level on the DoomWorld forums back in 2023, an unfinished, work-in-progress version of the house was found on a floppy disc gifted to him inside a box of his dead friend's belongings. A journal included in the download file explains more about the mod's somewhat difficult creation - an endeavour Veddge chose to undertake to honour his friend's memory. But the effort was undoubtedly worth it - as is the slight faff of getting Myhouse.wad to run if you're new to Doom things - and it serves as a simple but touching tribute to friendship across its ten minutes of nostalgic 90s FPS playtime. Only... what's that looking through the window on the ground floor? And was that door in the hallway always there?

Really, you could pluck any Rusty Lake game out of the 18 or so released across the series' ten years of existence, and you'd be in for a grimly macabre treat. But Servant of the Lake is developer Rusty Lake's latest offering, taking players back to 1839, where they've been hired to serve the troubled Vanderboom family across an increasingly strange three-day reunion. Servant of the Lake isn't quite as ambitious as some of the series' other games, such as 2022's excellent co-op mysteryThe Past Within. But what it lacks in structural and narrative experimentation, it makes up for in puzzles, serving up an enjoyably refined take on the series' deceptively clever mix of casual point-and-click adventuring, room-escape-style puzzling, and fascinatingly fragmented, centuries-spanning narrative. And oh yes, it's weird, as its bucolic vistas and gentle bird song gradually give way to blood and butchery, and the comforting logic of reality dims. Sure, it's more darkly amusing than outright disturbing, but Rusty Lake still calls for fresh meat this Halloween.

Probably not one for the faint of heart, Horses gained infamy after being banned by Steam and then Epic Games last year. It all unfolds across two weeks on a farm where humans are kept, masked and naked, in filthy captivity - a grim sight that goes completely unacknowledged for a surprisingly long time as you perform your daily tasks of gardening, woodchopping, and so on to satisfy the farmer's demands. Soon enough, though, Horses charges full-tilt into the grotesque. But while it'll probably make you gasp, and definitely make you squirm; its shocks are comparatively tame. Instead, writer and director Andrea Lucco Borlera's gleefully odd first-person narrative horror - developed in conjunction with Saturnalia studio Santa Ragione - gains its power from its wholly unique ambience, where surreal, slapstick comedy collides with arthouse experimentalism to create a thoroughly destabilising mood. All this, and it has something meaningful to say - not bad for £4.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

As a game, Hellraiser Revival is wobbly at best, particularly in its opening hours where its wonky gunplay and undercooked stealth never quite coalesce. That means its real-world bits - which include a lengthy stay in a dildo-strewn BDSM club - have a tendency to drag. But when the Labyrinth intermittently calls, developer Sabre Interactive pulls out all the stops. As Hellraiser Revival protagonist Aiden enters this confounding realm - an Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of piercing chains and endless, impossibly configured stone that serves as home to the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan - the dull, uneven combat gives way to puzzles, platforming, and wonderfully orchestrated pursuit sequences. And it makes the whole thing worthwhile. Slowly, as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs - and as Saber starts to have more fun with its combat tools - it gets considerably more engaging. Revival and its endless tableaus of horrifically rended flesh are definitely, absolutely not for the squeamish, but Hellraiser fans - and anyone looking for a bit of body horror nastiness - should get a kick out of this one.

Platforms: Meta Quest, PC, PS5, PSVR2, Xbox Series X/S, Switch

Back in 2023, Vertigo Games released a genuinely brilliant remake of developer Trilobytes' seminal 90s CD-ROM adventure, The 7th Guest, for VR. I loved it, and spent many happy hours roaming evil toymaker Henry Stauf's wonderfully eerie mansion, reimagined in new-fangled, fully explorable 3D. Its puzzle made some clever use of VR's 1:1 movement capabilities, and its cast - bringing to life the ill-fated guests of Stauf's macabre soiree - were a blast, hitting exactly the right level of camp and presented using some kind of volumetric witchcraft, letting you walk around their apparitions despite being live-action and FMV. It's great, spooky fun for puzzle fans - even if you're not familiar with the original - but its VR requirements meant it couldn't be enjoyed by all. Well, earlier this year, Vertigo released a non-VR version for Xbox, PS5, and PC. And while it loses a little in translation to flatscreens and standard controls, it's still an enjoyable way to enjoy a cult-classic.

Well, it's solitaire, isn't it? Only, that's not entirely true. Forbidden Solitaire is a clever bit of found media horror, inviting players to explore the titular CD-ROM game - an imagined relic of the short-lived 90s multimedia boom in which the games industry convinced itself the future was lurid colour palettes, awkward pre-rendered polygons, and juddery grainy FMV. Developer Night Signal Entertainment and Grey Alien Games capture the era perfectly as you begin to investigate the enigmatic game, which - as your sister quickly informs you over DM during the game's 2019-set narrative framing device - was embroiled in controversy on release, not least because of its disturbing links to gruesome unexplained deaths. Forbidden Solitaire's fictional history is told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, and even a pitch-perfect VHS recording of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show. But the majority of your time is spent playing Forbidden Solitaire itself, lost in a ghoulish labyrinth said to grant immortality to those that can reach the end. But of course all is not as it seems. Forbidden Solitaire is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn, and - wholly unexpectedly - plays a damn good game of solitaire too.

For a while, it looked like Routine might not make it. First announced in 2012, it vanished into the kind of development hell that rarely results in anything good. But Routine isn't just good, it's great; a cracking first-person sci-fi horror that's got a particularly old-school vibe. Routine's tale of ancient influences and rogue AI takes place on a retro-futuristic lunar resort where the lo-fi 80s tech lends proceedings a disorientatingly anachronistic flavour. Here, adverts for VHS recorders flash up on chunky CRT screens as you ride the sleek transportation train, and the mall, with its futuristic pre-fab curves, meets an explosion of neon and plastic palms. Routine is refreshingly unforthcoming about what to do and where to go; giving you a loose objective, your C.A.T. device - a wonderfully tactile gadget that's half maintenance gun, half PDA - then just sending you off to explore. Unfortunately, the resort is kaput; full of flickering lights and ominous shadows. Still worse are the Terminator-like security bots, always primed to give chase when they spy you - their relentless footsteps reaching a horrifying crescendo behind you. It's a game of claustrophobic stealth and panicked pursuits - and that's just for starters. You're about to have a very bad shift.

#10541. NASA just used satellites and debris to navigate without GPS

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly important as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

The FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

"FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," said Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing."

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points

The FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

During position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

FALCON then compared the catalog information with observations gathered by Starling's cameras. Using those measurements, it calculated Starling's position while also refining the estimated locations of other objects in space. The resulting estimates were even more precise than the existing catalog data.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation

FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

These abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an important role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology

The FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

Later this year, Starling, which launched in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

#10540. Viral steak ‘restaurant’ serves customers straight out of their apartment window

A new ‘restaurant’ has been going viral on social media, as customers are lining up to give steak served through a window in New York.

When a restaurant gets rave reviews and becomes pretty popular, it can be hard to get a reservation. That is especially true in New York, with some of the most popular restaurants having month-long waiting lists in order to get a table.

However, one of the newest ‘restaurants’ going viral doesn’t actually operate with tables, but there is still a reservation system. It’s called ‘Some Guy’s House,’ and it’s located in Brooklyn.

They only operate on Thursdays and Fridays, between five and eight in the evening, and every order comes out of a window through a custom-built pulley system. Seriously.

A post shared by Some guy’s house (@someguyshouse119)

As a result of the unusual concept, ‘Some Guy’s House’ has caught attention on social media – Instagram in particular – with customers needing to reserve a spot online before turning up to the window.

You can risk a walk-up, but with only 72 plates available on a Thursday, and 62 on a Friday, you might find yourself out of luck. A spot costs $25, and with that you get a steak, potato, and some spinach.

One New York-based influencer called it “unbelievable” after getting a taste for themselves too, showing that plenty of folks have been pulling up for a meal.

A post shared by Some guy’s house (@someguyshouse119)

This isn’t the first ‘restaurant’ from a house that the internet has thrown support behind. Back in April, a Norwegian pizza joint – Pizza from a balcony – went viral for selling slices to passersby.

Just like ‘Some Guy’s House’, Pizza from a balcony also delivers food using a pulley system, with some viewers being “jealous” that they couldn’t just walk up and experience it for themselves.
