#10429. Are American voters actually gloomy about the economy?

Polling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy.

At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish.

This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being.

This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important.

Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing.

These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures.

So what is going on?

As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power.

Reality vs. “vibes”

When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy—and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy—one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases.

This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being.

But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms.

Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment, and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index.

Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out.

But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then.

What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling—which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters.

Inequality vs. growth

One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence.

Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels.

This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation.

In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate.

This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed.

In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture.

It’s not just about me

When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents.

But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity, and economic justice.

When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.”

This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party.

Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole.

If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality.

Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it—it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in.

Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health—without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built—may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns.

Erin Kay Lockwood is an assistant professor of political science at the University of California, Irvine.

#10427. Google says Gemini 4 Argon ranks well behind Claude and GPT-6 for Android coding

Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models.

The Android Bench was introduced early this year as a way for Android developers to get a quick way to see what AI models were best suited to Android coding assistance based on a test from Google. That test took into account aspects of AI use that are specific to Android coding and best practices in Android development. As Google has continued its tests and ranking new models, it has also included the average cost as a part of the benchmark so that developers can make the best decision for their needs.

With the October 26 update, Google has added the reasoning level used for each model, as well as adding results for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, as well as Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon.

Currently topping the chart is Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a pass rate of 40% and a completion rate of 80.9%. Claude Opus 5.5, added to the list in early October, comes in second place.

OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol might be the most interesting addition here, coming in at a pass rate of 29.3% and completion rate of 82.8%, but a cost of just $99.50 compared to Claude’s $1,574.90 cost for its first place finish.

But it’s Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon that makes a rather underwhelming debut, sitting well behind other frontier models in fifth place. It lags behind Claude Fable 5.1 at a mere 21.3% pass rate, 81.8% completion rate, and an average cost of $267.70.

In a report shortly after Google’s announcement of Gemini 4 Argon, some internal voices claimed that the model “struggles to handle certain coding tasks,” though Google stood by its capabilities.

#10426. I auditioned 12 AI agents to be my chief of staff. Here’s how they compared

This article is republished with permission from Wonder Tools, a newsletter that helps you discover the most useful sites and apps.

I’ve never had a secretary before. Or a chief of staff. With these AI agents, I suddenly feel like I have both. This week, among other things, they:

  • Researched and booked Amtrak train tickets for me
  • Briefed me about important overnight emails and upcoming meetings
  • Surfaced an important contract I had overlooked
  • Turned my bookshelf into a visual reading list

Unlike older chatbots, these agents can take action proactively without waiting for a prompt. They can go online and research or buy things, make reservations, or fill in forms. They can look through various documents, transcripts, and emails to help you finish tedious projects.

Agents are the biggest step forward for AI this year. I’m testing a dozen to compare their reliability, features, and design: Thine, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, Town, Hark, Muse, Poke, Ambi, Sentience, Extra, Slashy, and Claude Duet.

My early favorites: Dots, Slashy, and Hark

  • Dots has helped me spot calendar conflicts and find and prepare materials I need for work. I use it several times a day.
  • Slashy has changed how I manage email. It’s a strong alternative to Superhuman, the email app I’ve used for years. Slashy puts an AI agent inside my inbox.
  • Hark has a standout design. It’s been reliable for shopping and reservations.

Other observations

  • Business agents will be a separate category. Town, for example, is easy to use and well designed, but its features are tuned to small businesses and midmarket companies.
  • These are early impressions. I’ll share more as the tools develop. I’m working on a post about Slashy and how to use AI to help with email overload. The inbox is where I see early agents being most helpful.

One is enough

Start with one agent that does what you need. I’m testing a bunch for now, but ultimately I’ll prioritize just a few with distinct strengths.

What they cost

Some agents, like Instinct, Hark, and Muse, start out free. Others require a paid subscription.

  • Dots is so far available only on ChatGPT’s Pro plan, which starts at $100/month.
  • Town starts free, but the Pro plan is $49/month.
  • Hark starts free. Upgrade for $20/month for more AI usage or $100/month for full power.
  • Thine is free to start. It’s $15/month or $120/year for extra capabilities.
  • Pricing for other agents is still taking shape. You can test many for free. Before connecting your accounts, check on ongoing costs and how each service uses your data.

Connect your email, calendar, and files

Thine and Dots became much more useful as soon as I connected them to my email, calendar, documents, and Granola meeting transcripts. Now they have a broad view of my projects for context, as well as a detailed understanding of my emails and tasks. Drawing on meeting transcripts, they even understand what I’ve promised to do.

2 reasons to try an AI agent

  • They save time, handling pesky tasks that used to take hours. Examples:
    1. Hark coordinated a tricky travel itinerary and handled the booking on Amtrak’s clunky site.
    2. Dots pulled a batch of related emails into a doc, a task that would otherwise have taken me 45 minutes.
  • They prevent headaches. They don’t wait for me to send a prompt. Numerous times they’ve helped me avoid costly errors. Examples:
    1. Dots found an appointment mentioned in a buried email and alerted me that it was missing from my calendar.
    2. Thine reminded me to send an important email I had forgotten.

5 differences between agents and chatbots

  1. They’re easier to get started with. Claude Code, Codex, and tools like Hermes Agent are at least as powerful as most agents I’m describing here, but they can seem intimidating. Setting them up is a bit like learning to use a manual camera. You have to figure out which connections to enable, which plugins to add, and which skills to install. Agents like Thine, Hark, and Town are more like point-and-shoot cameras. They guide you through setup and connections to your calendar, email, Notion, etc., with explanations in plain language.
  2. You text them like a person. Many agents, like Instinct, Poke, and Slashy, work in SMS, iMessage, or WhatsApp. So you don’t have to open an app or browser tab. It’s like messaging a colleague instead of walking over to the help desk.
  3. They reach out to you. Chatbots wait for your prompt. You might go days without remembering to use one. Agents send morning briefings, flag missing details on your calendar, and nudge you about unsent drafts. It’s the difference between a chief of staff who knocks on your door versus a reference librarian waiting at a desk.
  4. Flexible models. Most agents can switch among models from different AI providers, like travel agents who can book any airline. ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude rely primarily on their own models.
  5. You have one ongoing conversation, not hundreds of chats. I like how Thine and Dots keep a single long-running thread. Both remember our past conversations reliably. Chatbots I use scatter my history across lots of threads, which can make older exchanges hard to find.

The lines are blurring

For now the differences are noticeable, but major AI companies are adding similar capabilities. OpenAI’s Dots is already an excellent, if expensive, agent, and Claude Duet arrived on October 23.

I avoided the first generation of AI agents, like OpenClaw, because they seemed complex and risky. But several agents I’m testing are easy to use, and free to try.

What I hand off, and what I don’t

My goal isn’t to outsource my thinking or writing. I enjoy both. I want agents to handle background tasks like filing, organizing, and checking email for important messages. Or filling in annoying online forms. That leaves me more time to concentrate, with less worry that I might be missing an important message or task.

4 ways my AI chief of staff helps

1. Tame my inbox

I now get three times as many emails as I did three years ago. Many are AI-generated marketing or PR messages. With that email slop strewn across my three addresses, it’s easy to miss an important message among more than 1,000 emails a week. AI agents help me:

  • Summarize important new messages. At 8 a.m. my agents text me a summary of important emails from the previous evening and overnight. Instead of starting the day by scanning through hundreds of messages, I can just act on five important ones.
  • Handle irrelevant email for me. I respond myself to important and personal messages. But I don’t have the four hours it would take to reply to the hundreds of unsolicited, irrelevant emails I get every day. My agent can sort and archive those, or, in some cases, suggest quick “no, thank you” notes I can edit.

2. Plan my day

Mapping out my day at 8:30 a.m. means fewer decisions later, when I’m less focused, about what I should be doing.

My agents can look at my calendar, email, project materials, task list, and notes to suggest a detailed plan based on my preferences. They know I need breaks for stretching and meditation, a lunchtime walk, and time to call Mom. They use data from Rize, my time-tracking app, to estimate how long tasks usually take me.

During my Friday review, they help me reflect on next week’s priorities, tasks that need follow-up, and long-term projects to start. I head into the weekend feeling less stressed.

3. Research tricky decisions

In a day, I might have five to 10 questions an AI butler can help me research. I recently needed to turn 11 lengthy Google Docs into a printed book. I had to compare file conversion tools, check prices and reviews for book-printing services, and understand the technical steps.

That research would once have taken me an hour or more. This time I asked an agent to handle it and went back to preparing to teach. About five minutes later, my agent delivered an excellent recommendation in the Google Doc I’d requested.

I don’t like shopping. But I like knowing I’m getting a well-reviewed product or service at a good price. Hark and Instinct can compare options, recommend what to buy, and set up the purchase for me to confirm. Caveat: Check how free shopping agents make money, and whether their recommendations include paid placements.

4. Organize files

Connect an AI assistant to your files and work apps, like Google Drive, Slack, and Notion. Then ask it to move documents between folders. You can ask it to summarize document changes or ticket activity, or to create a new dashboard.

The hardest part is deciding what to delegate. I often ask my agents to suggest useful tasks they can handle. I tell them what tasks I find most annoying, what I enjoy doing myself, and what I can’t risk messing up.

Caveats

  • A new monthly bill. If you already pay for ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, adding another AI bill may seem extravagant. But for what will likely end up costing about $5 a week, you get a 24/7 assistant. If that saves you time and stress, it may feel worth it. As competition heats up, your main AI subscription may soon include an agent. For now, it’s like streaming. Netflix alone might be enough for some, but others happily pay for Hulu, Apple TV, and Disney+ too.
  • Expect periodic roadblocks. The services are still new. One told me it could send me a text, but not an email. Another said it could open docs from only one of my Google accounts. These annoyances can stall an otherwise useful task. Some problems have quick fixes. Others require workarounds while these services develop. I remember having to use two separate computers when dial-up Internet meant waiting minutes for each Web page to load.
  • Connecting your accounts can be a nuisance. Assistants need permission to access your accounts. That’s important for protecting your security. But it can create headaches when you have multiple Gmail accounts, extra sign-in steps, or workplace restrictions. I’m glad security protections prevent random people from logging into my accounts. But expect some setup friction.
  • Some won’t survive. For now, the money is flowing freely. Town raised $108 million this week at a $1 billion valuation and Instinct raised $1 billion recently. As individuals and businesses choose their agents, subscription fatigue may limit how many they’re willing to pay for.

The bottom line: If you haven’t yet experimented with an AI agent, start a free trial. Assign a few research, summarization, and shopping tasks. Judge it by the usefulness of its response, the time it saves, and how easy it is to use. Leave a comment to share your impressions.

#10424. Google Photos rolls out customizable redesign of your ‘Collections’ tab

Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS.

The previous design started with a 2×2 grid. Favorites and Trash were at the top, while the other two shortcuts changed based on usage. Then there were large cards for Albums, On this device, People & pets, Wardrobe, Documents, Places, Stickers, and Moments. On Android, this was followed by a list: Screenshots, Videos, Recently Added, Archive, and Locked.

This redesign of Collections is focused on customization. The first section is called “Pinned” and lets you choose which cards appear. By default, the carousel shows Favorites, Screenshots, and Trash. You also have the option to remove this section entirely.

That is a surprisingly deep customisation experience which isn't usual at all with current/recent Google products. Good!

That’s followed by carousels for On this device, Albums, People & pets, Wardrobe, Places, and Documents. “View all” at the top-right corner lets you jump straight to the full grid or list view. Other options let you hide each section and rearrange the order in which they appear.

The “Other Collections” grid rounds out this page: Favorites, Screenshots, Moments, Videos, Recently Added, Stickers, Creations, Archive, Locked, and Trash. The “Reorder” button is found at the very bottom.

This redesign is now widely rolling out with Google Photos 7.97 (Android) and 7.98 (iOS). Instead of the usual Force stop on Android, we’ve curiously been able to get this server-side update by restarting our devices and then opening the Photos app.
